To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

i-deals are granted by supervisors in the context of developmental, flexibility, and overload i-deals, which are influenced by employee initiative and the type of work, as well as by organizational obligations, respectively.
supervisors differentiated among i-deals regarding developmental, flexibility, and work‐load reduction i-deals.
i-deals are granted to employees with high levels of performance (H2a) and that employees with high levels and quality of i-deals are more committed and more motivated to perform (H2b and H2c).
In summary, our research is concerned with
how supervisors perceive i-deals, and what they consider as antecedents and consequences of i-deals for themselves and their employees.
the antecedents and consequences of i-deals from the perspective of the supervisors.
the question of how and under what conditions i-deals can be successfully implemented in an organization.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of the present research are consistent with the theoretical framework.
the i-deals literature is still in its early stage of development and that there is much to be done in order to further develop the theory and research on this phenomenon.
the results of this research study are not only important for the field of HRM but also for the field of management.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the i‐deals are not a panacea, but they can be an effective means to improve the quality of employment relations and to increase the performance of employees.
we have shown that i-deals are not a panacea for all organizational problems, but can be an important tool for the organization to increase the motivation of its employees, and to retain them.
idiosyncrasy in employment conditions can be a means to enhance employee well‐being.
The main takeaway from our work is that
supervisors are willing to grant idiosyncractic deals (i-deals) to employees if they are motivated to do so and have the resources to do so.
the use of idiosyncratically negotiated work arrangements is not necessarily a sign of a dysfunctional work setting, but rather can be a sign of a healthy and flexible work setting.
i-deals can be beneficial for both employees and employers, but they need to be carefully managed to ensure a positive outcome.
